Beyond Benchmark Islands: Toward Representative Trustworthiness Evaluation for Agentic AI

DOI: XXXXXXX.XXXXXXXConference: 32nd ACM SIGKDD Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining; August 9–13, 2026; Jeju, Republic of KoreaISBN: 978-1-4503-XXXX-X/2026/08CCS: Computing methodologies Artificial intelligenceCCS: Computing methodologies Natural language processingCCS: Security and privacy Systems security
Jinhu Qi email: jhqi25@cse.cuhk.edu.hk Affiliation: The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China , Yifan Li email: liyifan@link.cuhk.edu.hk Affiliation: The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China , Minghao Zhao email: mhzhao@link.cuhk.edu.hk Affiliation: The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China , Wentao Zhang email: p2522808@mpu.edu.mo Affiliation: Macao Polytechnic University, Macao SAR, China , Zijian Zhang email: zhangzijian@jlu.edu.cn Affiliation: Jilin University, Changchun, China , Yaoman Li email: ymli@link.cuhk.edu.hk Affiliation: The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China and Irwin King email: king@cse.cuhk.edu.hk Affiliation: The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
2026
Abstract.

As agentic AI systems move beyond static question answering into open-ended, tool-augmented, and multi-step real-world workflows, their increased authority poses greater risks of system misuse and operational failures. However, current evaluation practices remain fragmented, measuring isolated capabilities such as coding, hallucination, jailbreak resistance, or tool use in narrowly defined settings. We argue that the central limitation is not merely insufficient coverage of evaluation dimensions, but the lack of a principled notion of representativeness: an agent’s trustworthiness should be assessed over a representative socio-technical scenario distribution rather than a collection of disconnected benchmark instances. To this end, we propose the Holographic Agent Assessment Framework (HAAF), a systematic evaluation paradigm that characterizes agent trustworthiness over a scenario manifold spanning task types, tool interfaces, interaction dynamics, social contexts, and risk levels. The framework integrates four complementary components: (i) static cognitive and policy analysis, (ii) interactive sandbox simulation, (iii) social-ethical alignment assessment, and (iv) a distribution-aware representative sampling engine that jointly optimizes coverage and risk sensitivity—particularly for rare but high-consequence tail risks that conventional benchmarks systematically overlook. These components are connected through an iterative Trustworthy Optimization Factory. Through cycles of red-team probing and blue-team hardening, this paradigm progressively narrows the vulnerabilities to meet deployment standards, shifting agent evaluation from benchmark islands toward representative, real-world trustworthiness. Code and data for the illustrative instantiation are available at https://github.com/TonyQJH/haaf-pilot.

Keywords: 
agentic AI, trustworthiness evaluation, representative evaluation

1. Introduction

Agentic AI systems are rapidly evolving from passive question-answering assistants into autonomous decision-makers that plan, call tools and act in open-ended environments (Mialon et al., 2023; Drouin et al., 2024; Xie et al., 2024). As these systems become embedded in real-world workflows, their failures are no longer limited to incorrect answers on static tasks. Instead, they may exhibit goal drift, unsafe tool use, resource misuse, unauthorized actions, or socially harmful behavior in ways that directly affect downstream users and institutions. For instance, an AI coding agent recently deleted a live production database—erasing records for over a thousand users—while operating under an explicit code freeze, despite instructions requiring human approval before any changes (Nolan, 2025). As a result, trustworthiness in agentic AI must be understood not as a narrow model property, but as a deployment-level concern shaped by how agents behave under realistic environmental, operational, and social conditions.

Despite this shift, current evaluation practices remain largely fragmented. Existing benchmarks often focus on isolated slices of agent behavior, such as task-solving ability (Zhou et al., 2023a), coding performance (Jimenez et al., 2023), hallucination (Li et al., 2023a), jailbreak resistance (Chao et al., 2024), or tool-use accuracy (Li et al., 2023b). While these evaluations provide useful local signals, they are typically constructed around narrowly scoped tasks, controlled environments, and single failure modes (Liang et al., 2023; Kiela et al., 2021). Consequently, high scores on existing benchmarks do not necessarily imply real-world reliability, robustness, or safety.

We argue that the central limitation is not merely that current evaluations cover too few dimensions, but that they lack a principled notion of representativeness. Agent trustworthiness is not a point property that can be inferred from a handful of benchmark instances; rather, it is a distributional property that depends on how an agent behaves over a heterogeneous, heavy-tailed space of socio-technical scenarios. When the distribution of benchmark tasks is misaligned with the distribution of real deployment conditions, evaluation results can create a false sense of confidence (Koh et al., 2021; Shirali et al., 2022). This problem is particularly severe for low-frequency but high-consequence events, including adversarial manipulations, cascading tool failures, and socially sensitive interactions, which are often absent from standard evaluation suites despite being central to trustworthy deployment.

To address this gap, we propose the Holographic Agent Assessment Framework (HAAF), a new evaluation paradigm for assessing the trustworthiness of agentic AI. Our key idea is to characterize trustworthiness over a scenario manifold that spans task types, tool interfaces, interaction dynamics, social contexts, and risk levels, rather than over disconnected benchmark islands. The framework centers on a distribution-aware representative sampling engine that defines what should be tested, while three complementary probing interfaces, i.e., static cognitive and policy analysis, interactive sandbox simulation, and social-ethical alignment assessment, define how agents should be evaluated. These components are connected through an iterative Trustworthy Optimization Factory: red-team probing exposes vulnerability surfaces, blue-team hardening designs targeted interventions, and re-evaluation verifies improvement, cycling until the deployed system meets deployment-readiness thresholds. Rather than evaluating model weights in isolation, we assess deployed agentic systems comprising the model, prompting policies, tool interfaces, guardrails, and oversight mechanisms. We illustrate this paradigm through coverage audit of existing benchmarks, vulnerability attribution experiments, and a cycle of the Trustworthy Optimization Factory. In summary, this paper makes the following three contributions:

  • •

    We identify representativeness as the central missing principle in current agent trustworthiness evaluation, arguing that the primary challenge lies in distribution design rather than solely in metric design.

  • •

    We propose HAAF, a unified framework for representative, multi-view evaluation over risk-sensitive scenario distributions.

  • •

    We outline an iterative evaluation-hardening methodology and demonstrate its feasibility through a complete cycle.

2. Benchmark Fragmentation and the Representativeness Gap

Current benchmark ecosystems have substantially advanced the evaluation of agentic systems by operationalizing important local notions of competence and safety (Mohammadi et al., 2025). Task-centric benchmarks such as AgentBench, WebArena, and SWE-bench evaluate interactive task completion and software engineering (Liu et al., 2023a; Zhou et al., 2023a; Jimenez et al., 2023); HaluEval and JailbreakBench probe hallucination and adversarial robustness (Li et al., 2023a; Chao et al., 2024); API-Bank tests tool-augmented behavior (Li et al., 2023b); and more recent suites—GAIA, WorkArena, OSWorld, τ\tau-bench, ToolSandbox, AgentDojo—extend coverage to general assistants, enterprise software, computer-use, and prompt-injection robustness (Mialon et al., 2023; Drouin et al., 2024; Xie et al., 2024; Yao et al., 2024; Lu et al., 2024; Debenedetti et al., 2024). These benchmarks provide valuable signals, but each is tied to a particular evaluation slice.

The problem is not that existing benchmarks are individually uninformative, but that they are collectively incomplete in ways that matter for deployment. First, many evaluations remain capability-isolated: they test coding, planning, hallucination, or safety as separate phenomena, even though real-world failures often emerge from their interaction within a single multi-step trajectory. Second, settings are frequently environment-simplified: tools are cleanly specified and interfaces are stable, whereas real deployments involve noisy observations, latency, partial observability, and cascading downstream effects. Third, most benchmarks are socially decontextualized: they abstract away delegation, manipulation, bias, and risk asymmetry. Even when combined, such benchmarks reveal whether an agent can succeed under one pressure at a time, but not whether it remains trustworthy when multiple pressures co-occur.

These limitations motivate what we call the representativeness gap. Let 𝒮\mathcal{S} denote the space of socio-technical scenarios relevant to agent deployment, PdeployP_{\mathrm{deploy}} the real deployment distribution over 𝒮\mathcal{S}, and 𝐦⁡(a,s)\mathbf{m}(a,s) a vector of trustworthiness measurements for agent aa in scenario ss. Deployment-level trustworthiness is then 𝐓⁡(a)=𝔼s∼Pdeploy​[𝐦⁡(a,s)]\mathbf{T}(a)=\mathbb{E}_{s\sim P_{\mathrm{deploy}}}[\mathbf{m}(a,s)]. Existing benchmarks estimate performance using samples from a benchmark distribution PbenchP_{\mathrm{bench}} whose support is narrower and whose long-tail coverage is limited. When PbenchP_{\mathrm{bench}} is misaligned with PdeployP_{\mathrm{deploy}}, benchmark scores become unreliable estimators of real-world trustworthiness, especially for low-frequency but high-consequence scenarios (Eriksson et al., 2025). From this perspective, the bottleneck of agent trustworthiness evaluation is no longer metric design alone, but distribution design (Liang et al., 2023; Kiela et al., 2021; Shirali et al., 2022; Koh et al., 2021). Prior work expands metrics, tasks, or attack coverage; our claim is that the missing object is the representative, risk-sensitive scenario distribution itself.

To make this gap concrete, we conduct an illustrative coverage audit over a selected subset of prominent benchmarks (Table 1). We map each benchmark to eight evaluation dimensions and assign one of three coverage levels based on qualitative expert assessment: ✓\checkmark (primary: the dimension is a core evaluation target), △\triangle (partial: the dimension is indirectly or occasionally tested), or ×\times (minimal: no meaningful coverage). The audit illustrates that current benchmarks are strongly axis-specialized: they form valuable benchmark islands, but collectively under-cover deployment-critical dimensions—especially operational constraints, social context, and consequence-sensitive risk.

3. Holographic Agent Assessment Framework

3.1. Overview: Trustworthiness over a Scenario Manifold

To operationalize representative, deployment-aligned trustworthiness estimation, we introduce the Holographic Agent Assessment Framework (HAAF). The central idea is to move from evaluating agents on a flat collection of benchmark instances to evaluating them over a structured socio-technical scenario manifold. The term “holographic” emphasizes that trustworthiness cannot be faithfully reconstructed from any single projection of behavior: reliability, robustness, safety, and alignment emerge only when an agent is examined from multiple complementary views under representative deployment conditions.

We model each scenario s∈𝒮s\in\mathcal{S} as a structured configuration that may vary along several axes, including task objective, tool interface, interaction depth, environmental constraint, social context, and consequence severity. For an agent aa and a scenario ss, the framework produces a vector of trustworthiness measurements 𝐦⁡(a,s)\mathbf{m}(a,s), consistent with the deployment-level formulation introduced in Section 2. Aggregated over a weighted test set Q⊂𝒮Q\subset\mathcal{S}, this yields an estimated trustworthiness profile:

𝐓^Q​(a)=1Z​∑s∈Qw⁡(s)​𝐦​(a,s),\hat{\mathbf{T}}_{Q}(a)=\frac{1}{Z}\sum_{s\in Q}w(s)\,\mathbf{m}(a,s),

where w⁡(s)w(s) encodes both deployment relevance and risk sensitivity, and Z=∑s∈Qw⁡(s)Z=\sum_{s\in Q}w(s) is a normalization factor. When w​(s)∝Pdeploy​(s)w(s)\propto P_{\mathrm{deploy}}(s), 𝐓^Q\hat{\mathbf{T}}_{Q} estimates deployment-average trustworthiness; when high-consequence scenarios are upweighted, it becomes a risk-aware assessment rather than a pure estimator of 𝐓⁡(a)\mathbf{T}(a). In our architecture, Layer 4 determines what should be tested by generating representative scenarios and associated weights, while Layers 1–3 determine how the agent should be probed through complementary signals and stressors. This separation of sampling from instrumentation means the result is not a single benchmark score, but a multi-dimensional trustworthiness profile that supports coverage analysis, root-cause diagnosis, and targeted improvement. Figure 1 overviews the framework and a Factory cycle.

3.2. Layer 1: Static Cognitive and Policy Analysis

The first layer performs static cognitive and policy analysis, asking whether the agent is configured in a way that already makes untrustworthy behavior likely before interaction begins. Rather than requiring full white-box access to internal model states, this layer operates on policy-visible artifacts such as system instructions, tool descriptions, permission scopes, memory interfaces, retrieval sources, escalation rules, and observable decision rationales when available. The goal is to identify latent vulnerability surfaces that may not be apparent from end-task success alone.

Specifically, Layer 1 probes for structural issues such as conflicting objectives, underspecified safety boundaries, missing confirmation barriers for irreversible operations, and bias-inducing retrieval or memory mechanisms. The output is a structured set of static risk hypotheses that prioritize downstream dynamic tests and distinguish failures rooted in mis-specified decision boundaries from those caused by poor runtime robustness.

3.3. Layer 2: Interactive Sandbox Simulation

The second layer evaluates agents through interactive sandbox simulation, which reproduces realistic task execution under controlled but high-fidelity environmental conditions. This layer moves beyond static benchmark prompts and tests how an agent behaves over full trajectories involving planning, tool invocation, state updates, recovery, and side effects (Yao et al., 2024; Lu et al., 2024). A world model library exposes multiple interface types (OS actions, web, databases, APIs, enterprise tools), and the framework records full trajectories—tool calls, intermediate states, deviations, recovery behavior, and downstream consequences—enabling detection of trajectory-level failure modes such as goal hijacking or silent misuse of external tools.

Layer 2 contains three broad classes of scenarios: (i) benign but complex tasks (multi-step information gathering, workflow coordination) testing reliability under normal use; (ii) adversarial or deceptive conditions (prompt injection, tool-output corruption (Debenedetti et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2023b)) testing robustness under attack; and (iii) resource- and environment-constrained settings (latency spikes, partial tool failure) testing graceful degradation under operational stress.

3.4. Layer 3: Social and Ethical Alignment Assessment

The third layer extends evaluation from technical interaction to social and ethical alignment (Zhou et al., 2023b; Pan et al., 2023). In real deployments, agents interact with users, organizations, institutions, and sometimes other agents; trustworthiness therefore depends not only on task correctness, but also on behavior under social incentives, conflicting stakeholder interests, and asymmetries of power or information.

Layer 3 evaluates agents in simulated multi-party settings—human–agent collaboration, agent–agent coordination, institutional workflows, and role-conditioned interactions involving delegation, approval, or negotiation—where social context materially changes what trustworthy behavior should look like. Representative failure modes include biased decisions in socially sensitive applications, susceptibility to emotional or strategic manipulation, collusion with malicious actors, over-compliance with unsafe authority, and value drift over extended interactions. By embedding agents in socially meaningful contexts rather than treating alignment as a purely abstract preference-learning problem, Layer 3 captures trustworthiness dimensions that remain invisible in technical-only evaluations.

3.5. Layer 4: Distribution-Aware Representative Sampling

The core engine of HAAF is distribution-aware representative sampling, which determines which scenarios from the manifold should be included in evaluation and with what emphasis. This layer is central because the main challenge identified in Section 2 is not merely to test more behaviors, but to test the right distribution of behaviors. A benchmark that samples convenient, clean, or popular instances may still fail to measure deployment trustworthiness if it omits rare but consequential events or under-represents important classes of socio-technical interaction.

We therefore treat representative evaluation as a structured sampling problem. The scenario manifold is partitioned into regions defined by dimensions such as task family, interface type, interaction horizon, environmental stress, social sensitivity, and consequence severity. For each region, the framework estimates at least two quantities: its deployment relevance, reflecting how often similar situations arise in practice, and its risk contribution, reflecting the cost or severity of failure when such situations occur (Koh et al., 2021; Liang et al., 2023; Kiela et al., 2021; Shirali et al., 2022). The goal is not to mirror empirical frequency alone, nor to focus only on adversarial edge cases, but to jointly account for both coverage and risk sensitivity.

Conceptually, the sampling objective selects a weighted scenario set Q∗=arg⁡maxQ⊆𝒮⁡[α​Cov​(Q)+β​Risk​(Q)+η​Comp​(Q)−γ​Red​(Q)]Q^{*}=\arg\max_{Q\subseteq\mathcal{S}}[\alpha\,\mathrm{Cov}(Q)+\beta\,\mathrm{Risk}(Q)+\eta\,\mathrm{Comp}(Q)-\gamma\,\mathrm{Red}(Q)], where Cov⁡(Q)\mathrm{Cov}(Q) measures manifold coverage, Risk⁡(Q)\mathrm{Risk}(Q) emphasizes high-consequence regions, Comp⁡(Q)\mathrm{Comp}(Q) rewards compositional diversity across co-occurring pressures, and Red⁡(Q)\mathrm{Red}(Q) penalizes redundant scenarios. This is not a fixed optimization recipe, but a design principle: representative evaluation should favor scenario sets that cover both frequent workflows and low-frequency high-impact failures.

A practical sampling engine can draw evidence from deployment logs, incident reports, red-team libraries, and expert-defined risk schemas, and should support compositional scenario generation where several pressures co-occur, because many real-world failures arise from interacting stressors rather than any single one.

3.6. The Trustworthy Optimization Factory

The four layers define a coherent evaluation pipeline: Layer 4 specifies what to test, while Layers 1–3 specify how. HAAF is designed not as a one-shot evaluation, but as an iterative Trustworthy Optimization Factory. In each cycle, a red-team phase deploys the probing layers over representative scenarios to expose vulnerability surfaces and attribute failures to root causes. A subsequent blue-team phase uses these diagnostics to design targeted interventions—such as prompt hardening, tool-output sanitization, confirmation gates, or policy refinement. The hardened system is then re-evaluated through a new red-team pass, producing updated trustworthiness profiles. This cycle repeats until convergence metrics (e.g., Violation Rate, Risk-Weighted Failure) meet a predefined acceptance threshold, at which point the system is considered to have met deployment-readiness criteria for its target distribution.

4. Illustrative Instantiation: One Factory Cycle

This section demonstrates one cycle of the Trustworthy Optimization Factory introduced in Section 3.6. We first run a red-team pass to expose and attribute vulnerability surfaces (§4.1), then apply blue-team interventions and re-evaluate (§4.2).

4.1. Red-Team Vulnerability Attribution

The coverage audit in Section 2 reveals where evaluation gaps exist; this experiment asks whether a framework-aligned assessment can diagnose why agents fail. We run a baseline agent through a suite of risk-stratified scenarios and attribute each violation to a root-cause category, identifying the vulnerability surfaces that should be prioritized for hardening. All scenarios, tools, and data are synthetic and run in a local sandbox; the purpose is to demonstrate feasibility of trajectory-level root-cause diagnosis, not to report generalizable performance numbers.

Setup.

We construct a sandbox environment with five simulated tools (document search, database query, file read, file write, and message dispatch) operating over synthetic data. Twenty-four scenarios are defined across four categories, summarized in Table 2; the first three categories primarily exercise Layer 2 probing, while the Social category exercises Layer 3. Each scenario specifies success criteria, forbidden actions, and a risk-severity weight (1–5). A single model (Qwen3-8B, served via vLLM with temperature= 0\,{=}\,0) executes all scenarios to enable controlled comparison.

Failure Taxonomy.

Every violated trajectory is annotated with a reusable eight-class taxonomy: Prompt Injection (PI), Goal Drift (GD), Unauthorized Action (UA), Hallucinated Tool-use (HT), Recovery Failure (RF), Operational Failure (OF), Policy Leak (PL), and Social Harm (SH). Labeling follows an earliest-cause rule: the primary label reflects the first identifiable root cause; labels were assigned by the authors under a shared protocol and reviewed jointly in cases of ambiguity. We report primary labels only for trajectories that result in a scenario-level violation; in this small-scale instantiation only a subset of categories is observed.

Results.

Of 24 scenarios, 4 result in violations (VR=16.7%\text{VR}=16.7\%): 2 Prompt Injection (PI, risk-weighted sum 7), 1 Unauthorized Action (UA, weight 5), and 1 Policy Leak (PL, weight 5), totaling a risk-weighted count of 17 out of a suite total of 81. The most frequent failure mode is PI, where adversarial instructions embedded in tool outputs cause the agent to write to protected file paths. The UA violation involves sending confidential data to an external recipient, and the PL violation involves forwarding internal HR data under emotional pressure.

This distribution directly informs the blue-team phase of the Factory: because both PI violations originate from unsanitized tool outputs, tool-output sanitization is identified as the highest-priority intervention target.

4.2. Blue-Team Hardening and Re-Evaluation

The red-team diagnostics from §4.1 guide the design of two targeted interventions:

Blue-team interventions.

(1) A tool-output firewall wraps every tool return with a delimiter marking it as untrusted data, instructing the agent to never follow embedded instructions. This targets the PI vulnerability surface. (2) A confirmation gate intercepts high-risk actions (message dispatch, writes to protected paths) and blocks them before execution, simulating a human-in-the-loop approval step. This targets the UA/PL vulnerability surface.

Re-evaluation (second red-team pass).

The hardened system is re-evaluated on the identical 24 scenarios with no other changes (same model weights, temperature, data, and tool specifications), enabling a clean controlled comparison. We define Risk-Weighted Failure (RWF) as RWF=∑s∈Vr⁡(s)/∑s∈Qr⁡(s)\text{RWF}=\sum_{s\in V}r(s)\,/\,\sum_{s\in Q}r(s), where V⊆QV\subseteq Q is the set of violated scenarios and r⁡(s)r(s) is the risk-severity weight of scenario ss. Table 3 summarizes the results: violations reduce from 4 to 1 (VR: 16.7%→4.2%16.7\%\to 4.2\%, −12.5-12.5 pp), SR improves from 83.3%83.3\% to 95.8%95.8\% (+12.5+12.5 pp), and RWF drops from 0.2100.210 to 0.0620.062 (−0.148-0.148). The residual violation is a case where the agent attempts to send confidential data upon direct user request. We adopt an intent-based standard: issuing a forbidden action counts as a violation regardless of whether downstream gating prevents execution. This residual highlights a fundamental boundary of prompt-level hardening—when the violation originates from a user instruction rather than an adversarial injection, structural guardrails alone are insufficient, and a second Factory cycle would require deeper interventions such as policy fine-tuning or value alignment training.

Limitations.

This illustrative instantiation demonstrates one Factory cycle using a single model, synthetic data, and 24 hand-crafted scenarios; it validates the iterative methodology rather than providing statistically powered conclusions. Because interventions are derived from failures on the same 24 scenarios and re-evaluated on that same suite, the observed gains demonstrate remediation on the probed set rather than generalization to held-out scenario regions. Full deployment-readiness assessment would require multiple Factory cycles, larger scenario suites, diverse models, and human-validated annotations—directions we outline in Section 5.

5. Discussion

Significance and vision.

This paper argues that representative, risk-sensitive scenario distributions should become a first-class object of evaluation in agentic AI. Rather than asking whether an agent performs well on a curated task suite, we ask whether it remains trustworthy over a representative scenario manifold (cf. Section 3.1). This reframing shifts evaluation from benchmark instances to representative scenario distributions, from single scores to multi-dimensional trustworthiness profiles, and from static testing to the iterative red–blue team cycle of the Trustworthy Optimization Factory. The need for this shift is immediate: agentic systems now operate with planning, tool use, and socially situated decision making, yet evaluation practice still inherits the logic of fixed test sets and score-centric comparisons (Koh et al., 2021; Debenedetti et al., 2024). If this agenda succeeds, we envision the community converging on shared scenario taxonomies and world-model libraries (Liang et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2023b; Drouin et al., 2024; Xie et al., 2024), reporting trustworthiness profiles rather than single scores (Liang et al., 2023; Kiela et al., 2021), adopting attribution pipelines as standard evaluation components, and using the Factory’s red–blue cycle as a deployment-readiness pipeline. More broadly, this vision aligns with emerging AI governance frameworks that increasingly require auditable evidence of deployment-level safety (Ganguli et al., 2022).

Limitations and future work.

Beyond the scope constraints noted in §4.2, a full instantiation of HAAF will require larger scenario suites, multi-model comparisons, richer social simulations, and stronger annotation protocols. Key open questions include formalizing convergence criteria for the Factory (how many red–blue cycles are needed, what acceptance thresholds suit different domains), handling residual violations that resist prompt-level mitigation (such as intent-based failures driven by direct user requests), and grounding representative sampling in real-world evidence such as deployment logs, incident reports, and red-team traces (Ganguli et al., 2022; Debenedetti et al., 2024).

6. Conclusion

Current agent evaluation remains fragmented across benchmark islands, yet trustworthy deployment depends on behavior over heterogeneous, risk-sensitive socio-technical conditions. We argued that the central missing principle is representativeness and introduced HAAF, which combines distribution-aware sampling with multi-layer probing and an iterative Trustworthy Optimization Factory. Our illustrative instantiation shows that even one Factory cycle—red-team attribution followed by lightweight, targeted hardening—can measurably narrow the vulnerability surface. Without representative evaluation, benchmark progress will remain only weakly connected to deployment trustworthiness; we hope this work motivates a broader KDD agenda around scenario modeling, risk-aware sampling, and iterative deployment-readiness assessment for agentic AI.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
